title: Remember the sabbath
hookLine: rest as a gift for servants and animals too (Deuteronomy 5:14)

lines: THE SERVANT, THE STRANGER, THE DONKEY.
cards: Read the sabbath commandment slowly and look at who's on the list.

"Thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates." The children. The servants.
The stranger at the gate. The donkey. The day off isn't only for the one who owns the house.
Then Deuteronomy says why: "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou."

teach.b: The sabbath word comes in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, and the two give different reasons. Exodus points back to creation: God made the world and rested on the seventh day, so the people rest too.
Deuteronomy points back to slavery: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." Israel knew what endless work with no say was like. So, the reasoning goes, don't do it to anyone else.
On that reading, the sabbath isn't only private rest. It's a limit on the boss, including the boss you are.

teach.h: MADE FOR MAN, NOT MAN FOR IT.
teach.b: Jesus, criticized when his hungry disciples picked grain on the sabbath, answered, as day 166 heard: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift, not a trap.
Christians keep this commandment in different ways. Churches that gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, may call it the Lord's Day and treat it as their day of rest and worship.
Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday, the seventh day. Some Christians stop all paid work on their day; others mark it mainly with worship, family and a slower pace.
And the commandment was first given to Israel: in Jewish practice, Shabbat runs from Friday evening to Saturday evening.
Across all of them, Deuteronomy asks the same question: who gets to rest because of you, and who doesn't?

how: Christians who worship on Sunday keep it as the Lord's Day for worship and rest, while Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday; practice ranges from stopping all paid work to a day shaped mainly by worship and family.

games.q: you're one of Jesus's disciples, walking through a grainfield on the sabbath, and you're hungry. what happens in the story?
o: you go hungry until the sabbath ends.
you pick grain, and when critics object, Jesus defends you.
Jesus tells you to wait and fast.
games.why: the disciples pick grain, and Jesus answers the critics: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath."

practice: Bring to mind the people whose work makes your week possible, the one who cooks, drives, cleans, answers your messages, cares for your kids or your parents, and let one face come clear: someone who rarely gets a real break.
Think of one thing you could take off their plate, or one message you could hold until their workday is over. If you pray, you can name them before God.

wordCard.voice: Remember the sabbath. A day of rest, given not only to you but to everyone who works for you, the stranger, and even the animals.
